title: Saul and the Medium of Endor
summary: As the Philistines gather for war, Achish tells David he must march with them. Saul, terrified by the Philistine army and getting no answer from the LORD, disguises himself and goes by night to a medium at Endor, asking her to bring up Samuel. Samuel appears, repeats the judgment already pronounced on Saul, and tells him that tomorrow he and his sons will be with him; Saul collapses, and the woman feeds him a last meal before he goes out into the night.
story: The book has been moving toward this moment since Samuel first told Saul that the LORD had rejected him as king (chapter 15). Samuel has died (25:1), and the narrator repeats the notice here to remind us that the prophet who guided and rebuked Saul is gone. The Philistines are about to fight the decisive battle, and David, oddly, is marching with them. Saul, who had spent years chasing David instead of fighting Israel's enemies, now faces those enemies with no word from God. The chapter is the last scene of Saul's inner life before his death, and it ends with a haunting picture: a condemned king eating a meal prepared by a woman his own law had outlawed, then walking out into the dark.
historical:
The armies have moved north. The Philistines camp at Shunem on the north side of the Jezreel Valley, and Saul camps on Mount Gilboa to the south (in chapter 29 the narrator goes back to show the Philistines first mustering at Aphek). Controlling this broad valley meant controlling the main routes through the land, and a Philistine victory here would cut the northern tribes off from Saul's heartland. Endor lies north of Shunem, near the hill of Moreh and Mount Tabor, which means Saul had to slip around or behind the Philistine positions to reach it, a dangerous trip made at night and in disguise.

The notice that Saul had removed the mediums and spiritists from the land reflects the law of Moses, which forbade consulting the dead (Leviticus 19:31, 20:27; Deuteronomy 18:10-12). Saul's zeal in enforcing it earlier makes his visit now all the more damning. First Chronicles 10:13-14 later sums up his death as the result of his unfaithfulness, including consulting a medium instead of inquiring of the LORD.
cultural:
Necromancy, the practice of calling up the dead for knowledge of the future, was widespread in the ancient Near East. Mesopotamian and Hittite texts describe rituals for summoning spirits, sometimes through a pit dug in the ground, and some scholars connect the Hebrew word for medium with such a pit. Israel's law banned it because it sought guidance from a source other than the LORD and treated the dead as powers to be consulted. The LORD's normal ways of answering, which Saul lists, were dreams, the Urim (sacred lots kept with the priest's ephod), and prophets. Saul had cut himself off from the priesthood by massacring the priests of Nob (chapter 22), and the surviving priest with the ephod, Abiathar, was with David.

The woman calls what she sees elohim, a word normally meaning God or gods, which could also be used of spirits from beyond the living world (compare Isaiah 8:19). Samuel is recognized by his robe, the prophet's garment that had torn in Saul's hand when Samuel announced the kingdom would be torn from him (15:27-28). The meal at the end is a full act of hospitality: a fattened calf slaughtered and bread baked without waiting for leaven to rise, the kind of meal a host prepared for an honored guest in haste.
literary: The chapter frames the Endor scene with the Philistine threat (verses 1-2 and 4-5) and closes with the meal, so that the encounter with Samuel sits at the center. It is full of reversals and echoes. Saul swears by the LORD to protect a practice the LORD forbade. The prophet who anointed Saul now appears to announce his death. Samuel's words repeat his earlier judgments almost exactly, above all the image of the kingdom torn out of Saul's hand and given to his neighbor (15:28), and the reason, his failure to carry out the LORD's judgment on Amalek. There is also wordplay on Saul's name, which sounds like the verb to ask: Saul the asked-for king asks of the LORD and gets no answer, then asks a medium. The chapter ends in darkness, “And that night they got up and left.”

outline.t: David is called to march with Achish
Saul goes to the medium of Endor

doctrines.note: God speaks to his people in the ways he has chosen, and his silence can itself be a judgment. Saul seeks knowledge by a forbidden route and gets only the same word he had refused to heed. The chapter warns against trying to force guidance from God by any means at hand.

Consulting the dead was a form of turning from the LORD to other powers, and Israel's law treated it as spiritual unfaithfulness. Saul's descent shows how a person who once opposed such practices can reach for them in panic when obedience has already been abandoned.

Samuel's message is not new; it confirms what God had already said. Judgment here is the working out of Saul's long refusal to obey. The chapter also shows that God's word stands even when delivered in the strangest of settings.

words.note: Ov, a medium or the spirit of the dead that a medium consults. The word can refer both to the practitioner and to the ghost, and some scholars link it to a pit used in rituals for calling up the dead. It appears five times in this chapter, always under the shadow of the law that banned it.

Elohim, the ordinary word for God or gods. The woman uses it for the figure she sees rising from the earth, meaning a spirit or supernatural being rather than a deity to be worshiped. The usage shows the word's range and warns against reading every elohim as a claim about a god.

Urim, one of the two sacred lots (with the Thummim) kept by the high priest in the breastpiece of the ephod (Exodus 28:30) and used to ask the LORD yes-or-no questions. Its failure here means the ordinary priestly channel of guidance has gone silent for Saul.

Shaal, to ask or inquire, the verb from which Saul's name (Shaul, asked for) is formed. The people asked for a king, and Saul was the answer to their asking. Now he asks the LORD and hears nothing, and the pun marks the tragedy of the king who began as Israel's request and ends asking in vain.

christ: The chapter's contribution to the story that leads to Jesus is by contrast. Saul, the first anointed king, dies estranged from God, having sought light in darkness. The Bible's hope moves on to David and then to the son of David who would be the perfect king. The New Testament also speaks directly to the fear that drives Saul to Endor, the fear of death. Hebrews 2:14-15 says Christ shared our flesh so that by his death he might destroy the one who has the power of death and free those held in slavery by the fear of death. Where Saul sought a word from the dead in the dark, Christians confess that the risen Christ holds the keys of death (Revelation 1:18) and needs no medium to speak. This is a thematic connection, not a prediction in the chapter itself.

hard.q: Did Samuel really come back from the dead at a medium's call?
hard.a: Interpreters have given three main answers. Many, ancient and modern, hold that God really permitted Samuel to appear. They note that the narrator calls the figure Samuel, that his words come true, and that the woman herself seems shocked, as if something happened that she did not expect or control. The Jewish book of Ben Sira (Sirach 46) says Samuel prophesied even after death. Others, including a number of early Christian writers, argued that a deceiving spirit impersonated Samuel, since God would not honor a forbidden practice. A third view sees the whole scene as the medium's performance, though this struggles to explain the accurate prophecy. Early Christian opinion was divided, and the text does not explain the mechanism. What it makes plain is that the practice is condemned, that the appearance brings Saul no help, and that God's word through Samuel stands. The chapter gives no support to seeking contact with the dead.

questions: Saul enforced God's law when it cost him nothing and broke it when he was afraid. Where does fear tempt you to abandon convictions you once held firmly?
God's silence toward Saul was the result of Saul's long refusal to listen. How should a person respond when God seems silent?
The medium shows Saul kindness at the end, feeding him before his last battle. What do you make of mercy appearing in such an unexpected place?
